title: Optimisation: where the derivative is zero
intro: A company maximises profit, an engineer minimises material use — and a machine learning model minimises its loss. All three do the same thing: a function whose value depends on choices you make, and the question “which choice gives the best value?”. Differential calculus supplies the tool: on a smooth function a maximum or minimum can only sit where the slope vanishes — \( f'(x) = 0 \) — or on the boundary of the allowed region. This topic builds the complete method: finding critical points, classifying them with the first and second derivative, checking the boundaries, and — when the equation cannot be solved — letting gradient descent search. Exactly the path every ML model walks.
keyPoints: Extrema of a smooth function on a closed interval can only sit at critical points (\( f'(c) = 0 \) or \( f' \) does not exist) or on the boundaries of the domain — nowhere else.
First-derivative test: if \( f' \) switches from + to − at a critical point it is a local maximum; from − to + a local minimum; no sign change, no extremum (like \( x^3 \) at 0).
Second-derivative test: \( f''(c) > 0 \) means bowl-shaped → minimum; \( f''(c) < 0 \) means dome-shaped → maximum; \( f''(c) = 0 \) → the test is silent, fall back on the first test.
The word-problem recipe: (1) translate into a formula, (2) note the domain, (3) solve \( f' = 0 \), (4) test candidates AND boundaries, (5) state the answer in a sentence with units.
When \( f' = 0 \) cannot be solved analytically: gradient descent — repeatedly step against the slope, \( x \leftarrow x - \eta f'(x) \). That is exactly how every ML model minimises its loss.

blocks.html: Optimisation problems are recognisable by their shape, and the shape is always the same: there is an objective function (profit, volume, error, loss) depending on choice variables (price, dimension, model weights), and a domain of allowed choices (budget, available cardboard, reachable parameter values). Question: which choice optimises the objective? The calculus reflex is old but load-bearing: on a smooth function a peak or valley cannot be tilted. If the slope at your highest point still points downhill, you were not at the top — keep walking. At an interior extremum the tangent must therefore be horizontal: \( f'(c) = 0 \).

One distinction that recurs on every exam and in all practice: local versus global. A local maximum is only higher than its immediate surroundings — climb a hill in the Alps and you locally tower over everything, even though Everest is taller. A global maximum is the highest point of the entire domain. For convex functions (bowl-shaped everywhere, \( f'' \geq 0 \)) the two coincide: one valley, no surprises — the squared loss of linear regression has exactly that shape, which is why that loss is so beloved. For non-convex functions (neural networks) both kinds coexist and a naive search strategy can get stuck on a local hill.

Terminology for the rest of this topic: extremum is the collective name for maximum and minimum; a critical point is any interior candidate (\( f' = 0 \) or non-differentiable); an inflection point is where the curvature changes sign. And remember that “maximising \( f \)” is the same as “minimising \( -f \)” — ML almost always speaks of minimising a loss, but every technique here works directly by flipping a sign.

Collecting the candidates is mechanical: differentiate, set to zero, solve. Take the parade example \( f(x) = x^3 - 3x \): \( f'(x) = 3x^2 - 3 \), so \( 3x^2 - 3 = 0 \) gives \( x = \pm 1 \). There are no other candidates — and together with the domain boundaries (if bounded) that is the complete list where an extremum can live. In the plot below you walk the curve with the xc slider and see both functions at once: the cyan curve is \( f \), the yellow curve is \( f' \). The status chip translates the slope into words — and at \( x = \pm 1 \), exactly where the yellow curve crosses the x-axis, it flips from “increasing” to “decreasing” (or vice versa).

blocks.title: f and f′ in one view
blocks.subtitle: Slide xc along the cubic f(x) = x³ − 3x (cyan) and watch the slope chip move; the yellow curve is the derivative f′(x) = 3x² − 3. Where the yellow curve crosses the x-axis (x = −1 and x = 1) the slope is zero — those are the critical points. The status chip reads f′ as language.

blocks.html: Reading off what the critical points mean: at \( x = -1 \) sits the hilltop (\( f(-1) = 2 \), local maximum) and at \( x = 1 \) the valley floor (\( f(1) = -2 \), local minimum). But note the third characteristic spot: at \( x = 0 \) the curve is smooth yet horizontally gliding — no extremum, because the curve simply keeps descending through it. A critical point is a candidate, not yet a verdict; classification is the next step. That distinction matters: not every zero of \( f' \) is a peak or valley.

sections.title: Rising, falling and the first test

blocks.html: The sign of \( f' \) is the complete motion description of \( f \). Positive slope means rising (moving right, the values go up), negative means falling, zero means parallel to the x-axis. To classify a critical point you therefore look not at the point itself but at what happens around it — exactly what the first-derivative test formalises: compare the sign of \( f' \) just left and just right of the critical point. The four possible outcomes are in the table; the fourth (no switch) is the one exams and interviews set as a trap.

In practice you do this with a sign chart: list the zeros of \( f' \), pick one probe point in each intermediate interval, and record the sign of \( f' \) there. The chart then reads like a weather report for the curve: rising and falling stretches alternating at the critical points. For the cubic in the plot: the correct chart is rising on \( (-\infty, -1) \), falling on \( (-1, 1) \), rising on \( (1, \infty) \): first the hilltop, then the valley — and \( x = 0 \) sits in the middle of the falling stretch, which is why it is not an extremum. (Check it with the slider: at \( x = -2 \) the chip reads \( f' = +9 \), so the curve really is rising there.)

For a global maximum or minimum on a closed interval \( [a, b] \) you check three categories: the critical points inside the interval, plus the two endpoints — evaluate \( f \) at all candidates and the largest/smallest number wins. This candidate list is the complete, proven method: smooth functions can have an extremum on \( [a, b] \) nowhere else. Classic trap: forgetting the boundaries — precisely there, in word problems, the real answer often lives (as with the box below, where \( x = 15 \) on the boundary yields zero volume).

sections.title: Bending: concavity and the second test

blocks.html: The second derivative adds a second reading layer. Where \( f'' > 0 \) the function is convex (bowl-shaped — the tangents lie below the curve, like \( x^2 \)); where \( f'' < 0 \) it is concave (dome-shaped — the tangents lie above, like \( -x^2 \)); where the sign flips sits an inflection point. For the cubic \( x^3 - 3x \), \( f''(x) = 6x \): concave left of zero, convex right, inflection at the origin — watch the f″ metric in the plot above move and switch sign exactly at \( x = 0 \).

rows: local minimum — the lowest point of the bowl
local maximum — the top of the dome
test is silent — fall back on the first-derivative test

blocks.html: Why the second test is often faster: it only asks for \( f'' \) at the critical point itself — no probe points left and right, no sign chart. The intuition is physical: a critical point means “momentarily at rest” (slope zero), and the second derivative is the acceleration. Positive acceleration at the resting point: you are at the bottom and it goes up — minimum. Negative acceleration: you are at the top and it sinks away — maximum. The limitation is real: at \( f''(c) = 0 \) it says nothing (check \( x^4 \): \( f''(0) = 0 \) and yet a minimum), and then the first test is the only way out.

For ML, concavity is not a side note but the heart of the learning process. A convex loss (linear regression with squared loss, logistic regression with log-loss) has one valley: any descent strategy eventually finds the global minimum — slowly perhaps, but surely. A non-convex loss (neural networks) has multiple valleys and plateaus: gradient descent can strand in a local minimum, and the choice of initialisation suddenly matters. And the learning rate is a concavity issue: in a narrow, steep valley (large \( f'' \)) big steps bounce you between the walls — see Gradient descent for the simulation.

sections.title: A classic problem: the cardboard box

blocks.html: Now the entire repertoire in one AP-style word problem. From a square sheet of cardboard 30 by 30 cm you cut an \( x \times x \) square from each corner and fold up the sides into an open box. Which \( x \) gives the largest volume? Translate into formulas first: the base becomes \( (30-2x) \times (30-2x) \), the height becomes \( x \), so the volume is the product of all three. The domain is forced by physics: \( x > 0 \) (otherwise no height) and \( x < 15 \) (otherwise no base) — so \( x \in (0, 15) \).

blocks.label: Box volume
blocks.caption: height × width × depth. A cubic function of the cut size — at both ends of the domain the volume goes to zero, so the maximum is guaranteed to sit inside.

blocks.html: Differentiate with the product rule (since it is \( x \) times a square): \( V'(x) = (30-2x)^2 + x \cdot 2(30-2x) \cdot (-2) \). Factor out \( (30-2x) \) and it falls into place: \( V'(x) = (30-2x)\left[(30-2x) - 4x\right] = (30-2x)(30-6x) \). Zeros: \( x = 15 \) (boundary of the domain, volume zero) and \( x = 5 \) — the only interior candidate. Second test: \( V''(x) = 24x - 240 \), so \( V''(5) = -120 < 0 \): concave at the top. Maximum at \( x = 5 \), with volume \( V(5) = 5 \cdot 20^2 = 2000 \) cm³.

blocks.title: Volume against the cut size
blocks.subtitle: Slide the cut size x and hunt for the maximum: at x = 5 cm the volume chip lights up green — exactly the answer from the analysis. Note the slope chip V′: positive left of the maximum (more volume available), exactly zero at the top, negative after (you are cutting too much away).

blocks.html: The plot reads back the whole analysis. Left of 5, \( V' > 0 \): cutting larger yields (still) more volume — the curve rises. At \( x = 5 \) itself the slope is exactly zero: the yellow dot sits on the top of the cyan curve, at height 2000. To the right \( V' < 0 \): every extra centimetre of cutting costs volume, and as \( x \to 15 \) a bottomless strip of zero remains. The sharp observation that turned the word problem into a calculus problem: the two physical boundaries are both terrible (volume 0), so the optimum must sit inside — and inside, it can only be where \( V' = 0 \).

This pattern — bad boundaries, smooth interior, hence a critical point — is why optimisation problems almost always take this shape. Whether it is a box, a fence of fixed length or a loss landscape: bound your domain honestly, accept that the edges are usually disastrous, and the only remaining question is “where does the derivative vanish?”. On the AP exam this format returns almost every year, dressed in different props.

sections.title: Searching without a formula: gradient descent

blocks.html: Until now we solved \( f'(x) = 0 \) analytically — factor out, take roots, done. But try that on \( f(x) = e^{-x} + x^2 \) or, worse, on the loss of a neural network with a million weights: no closed form, no symmetry to the rescue. Then you flip the approach: you do not need to know where the slope becomes zero, you only need to follow it. Standing on a slope that points downhill (\( f' < 0 \)), walk right; does it point uphill (\( f' > 0 \)), walk left. Both cases in one line: a step in the direction against the slope.

blocks.label: Gradient-descent update
blocks.caption: η (eta) is the learning rate: the step size. In higher dimensions f′ becomes the gradient ∇f and the rule stays literally the same — see Gradient descent.

blocks.html: A small, complete example: \( f(x) = x^2 - 4x + 5 \), so \( f'(x) = 2x - 4 \), and analytically you see immediately that the minimum sits at \( x = 2 \). Start gradient descent at \( x_0 = 5 \) with \( \eta = 0{,}1 \): each step becomes \( x \leftarrow x - 0{,}1(2x-4) = 0{,}8x + 0{,}4 \). The distance to 2 shrinks by a factor 0.8 per step — measurable, predictable, and after 35 steps you sit at 2.001; after a few hundred steps the distance to the exact minimum is numerically zero. No derivative-zero solved, and still the minimum found: that is the embrace that makes training models with millions of parameters possible at all.

blocks.caption: gradient descent finds the parabola's minimum
blocks.source:
# f(x) = x^2 - 4x + 5  ->  f'(x) = 2x - 4  ->  minimum at x = 2
x, eta = 5.0, 0.1
for step in range(35):
    x = x - eta * (2*x - 4)     # one step against the slope
    if step % 5 == 0:
        print(f'step {step:2d}: x = {x:.4f}   f(x) = {x*x - 4*x + 5:.4f}')
print(f'after 35 steps: x = {x:.4f}  (exact minimum: x = 2)')

blocks.html: Typical output: 4.4000, 2.7864, 2.2577, 2.0844, 2.0277, 2.0091, 2.0030 — and after 35 steps 2.0012. Each step does exactly what the theory promises: shrink the distance to 2 by a factor 0.8 (check it yourself: 3.0, 2.4, 1.92, ...). And encouragingly: a larger \( \eta \) goes faster — until it flips: at \( \eta > 1 \) the factor turns negative-ish and the sequence jumps all over the place. That instability is not a Python joke but the divergence from Gradient descent, in miniature.

blocks.caption: the box problem numerically: scipy as a second opinion
blocks.source:
from scipy.optimize import minimize_scalar

def V(x):
    return x * (30 - 2*x)**2        # the box volume

# minimise -V on the physical domain (0, 15)
res = minimize_scalar(lambda x: -V(x), bounds=(0, 15), method='bounded')
print(f'optimum at x = {res.x:.4f} cm')
print(f'maximum volume  = {-res.fun:.1f} cm^3')
print('the analysis said: x = 5, V = 2000')

blocks.html: Typical output: x = 5.0000, V = 2000.0 — the numerical search engine and the manual calculus give the same answer to four decimal places. That is how it works in practice too: analysis delivers insight and exact answers where possible; scipy.optimize (or gradient descent, or your DL framework's solver) delivers answers where the algebra stalls. Both angles belong to the same craft.

Zoom out and you see the entire ML workflow reflected in this topic. The loss is the objective function (how badly the model predicts on the training data); the weights are the knobs; the gradient is the derivative in many dimensions; and training = repeatedly applying \( x \leftarrow x - \eta \nabla f(x) \) until the loss will not fall further. What you practised here on one variable — critical points, convexity, learning-rate-versus-stability — scales directly to a million dimensions. Gradient descent treats the full version.
